name: meridian-support-kb-v1
description: A hand-built fixture, not an external benchmark. Twenty-five queries over ten short documents about an invented product, written by the authors of the retriever they grade. Use it to check that the pipeline works and that the arms differ - never as evidence of how this system would rank real traffic. BEIR / MS MARCO / LoTTE are the external standards; none of them runs offline in CI with no download, which is the only reason this file exists.

documents.text:
# Meridian billing

## Payment methods
Meridian accepts credit cards and, on annual plans, bank transfer. A card is
charged in the currency of the workspace. Adding a second card does not change
which one is charged: the primary card is used until you promote another one.

## Invoice schedule
Invoices are issued on the first day of each billing period and fall due within
fourteen days. The invoice PDF is attached to the notification email and is also
available under Settings, Billing, Invoices.

## Refunds and credits
A refund returns money to the original payment method and takes five to ten
business days to appear. A credit is applied to the next invoice instead and is
immediate. Support can issue a credit; only an owner can request a refund.

## Failed payments
When a charge fails, Meridian retries after one, three and seven days. The
workspace stays active during that window. After the third failure the workspace
drops to the free tier and existing keys keep working at free-tier quotas.

## Changing your plan
An upgrade takes effect at once and is prorated against the days remaining in the
period, so you are never charged twice for the same days. A downgrade takes
effect at the end of the current period and you keep paid features until then.

# Authentication

## API keys
An API key is a bearer token sent in the Authorization header. Keys are scoped to
one workspace and one environment. A key is shown once, at creation: Meridian
stores only a hash of it, so a key you did not copy cannot be shown again and has
to be replaced.

## Rotating a key
Create the replacement first, deploy it everywhere, and only then revoke the old
one. Revocation takes effect at once and cannot be undone. Holding both keys
valid for a window is what avoids a gap in service.

## OAuth device flow
A machine with no browser authenticates with the device flow: the client prints a
short code and a URL, a human approves it elsewhere, and the client exchanges the
code for a token. The code expires after ten minutes.

## Session lifetime
A browser session lasts thirty days and is extended on use. Signing out on one
device leaves the others signed in; use Revoke all sessions for that.

## Two-factor authentication
Time-based one-time passwords and hardware security keys are both supported. An
owner can require two-factor for every member, which signs out the members who
have not yet enrolled.

# Error codes

## ERR_4021 rate limit exceeded
The workspace has spent its request budget for the current window. The response
carries a Retry-After header in seconds. Retrying before that header expires does
not reset the window and does not help.

## ERR_4010 invalid credential
The bearer token was missing, malformed or revoked. This is not a permission
problem: the request was never associated with a workspace at all.

## ERR_4033 permission denied
The credential is valid, but the role attached to it may not perform this action.
Check the role the key was created with, not the key itself.

## ERR_5002 upstream timeout
A dependency did not answer within the deadline. This is a server-side fault and
is safe to retry with backoff, because the request was not applied.

## Retry guidance
Retry ERR_5002 with backoff, and ERR_4021 after Retry-After. Never retry ERR_4010
or ERR_4033 unchanged, because nothing about the request will have changed.

# Rate limits

## Default quotas
The free tier allows sixty requests per minute per workspace. The team tier
allows six hundred per minute, and enterprise is negotiated. Quotas are counted
per workspace and not per key, so issuing more keys does not buy more capacity.

## Burst allowance
A token bucket refills continuously and holds up to twice the per-minute quota,
so a short spike is absorbed. Traffic that stays above the quota is rejected once
the bucket empties.

## How limits are counted
Every accepted request costs one token. Rejected requests cost nothing. A
streaming response is counted once, at the moment the stream opens, however long
it stays open.

## Requesting a higher limit
An owner can ask for an increase from Settings, Usage. Say what sustained rate
you need and over what window. Increases are granted for one named environment
rather than for the whole account.

# Webhooks

## Registering an endpoint
Register one HTTPS URL per environment. Meridian sends a POST with a JSON body
and expects a 2xx within five seconds. An endpoint that answers slowly is treated
exactly like one that answers with an error.

## Signature verification
Every delivery carries a signature header, computed as HMAC-SHA256 over the raw
request body with the endpoint secret. Verify against the raw bytes: parsing the
JSON and serialising it again changes the body, and the signature will not match.

## Retry and backoff
A failed delivery is retried with exponential backoff for twenty-four hours.
After that the delivery is dropped and the endpoint is marked unhealthy until you
re-enable it.

## Replay protection
The signature header includes a timestamp. Reject any delivery whose timestamp is
more than five minutes old, or a captured request can be sent to you again later
and will still verify.

# Single sign-on

## SAML setup
Upload the identity provider metadata XML, then configure the assertion consumer
service URL that Meridian shows you. The email claim is the join key, so the
address in the directory has to match the address on the member.

## SCIM provisioning
SCIM keeps the member list in step with the directory: creating a user there
creates a member here, and deactivating one there takes that member's access
away. SCIM needs its own token, separate from any API key.

## Just-in-time creation
Without SCIM, a member is created the first time they sign in through the
identity provider. Just-in-time creation can only add people, never take anyone
away, which is why offboarding needs SCIM.

## Disabling password login
Once single sign-on is enforced, password login is refused for everyone except
break-glass owners, who keep it so that a broken identity provider cannot shut
the whole workspace out.

# Data export and deletion

## Requesting an export
An owner starts an export from Settings, Data. The job runs in the background and
the notification email carries a signed download link when it finishes.

## Export formats
Exports are newline-delimited JSON, one record per line, gzipped. CSV is offered
for tabular resources only, because a nested record cannot be written to CSV
without losing its structure.

## Retention of export files
A download link stays valid for seven days, after which the file is removed from
storage. Starting a new export does not extend the life of an older file.

## Deleting your data
Deleting a workspace schedules erasure after a thirty-day grace period, and an
owner can cancel at any point inside it. Once the grace period ends the data
cannot be brought back by anyone, support included.

# The Meridian command line tool

## Installing the tool
Install from your platform package manager, or download the static binary. The
binary carries no runtime dependencies, so it can be dropped straight onto a
build image without installing a language runtime first.

## Logging in
Run meridian login to start the device flow. In continuous integration, where
nobody can approve a code, set MERIDIAN_TOKEN in the environment instead.

## The deploy command
meridian deploy uploads the build and shifts traffic once the health check
passes. Pass --environment to aim at somewhere other than production.

## The logs command
meridian logs streams from the selected environment and accepts --since and
--grep. A stream counts as one request against the rate limit.

## The configuration file
meridian.toml at the repository root holds the default environment and the health
check path. A flag on the command line always beats the file.

# Deployments

## Environments
Every workspace has production and staging, and can add named preview
environments. An API key belongs to exactly one of them, which is what stops a
staging key from reaching production data.

## Zero-downtime releases
A release starts new instances beside the old ones and shifts traffic only after
the new instances report healthy. Old instances are drained rather than killed,
so requests already in flight finish normally.

## Health checks
The health check path is polled every ten seconds and has to answer 200 within
two seconds. Three consecutive failures mark an instance unhealthy and take it
out of rotation.

## Rolling back
A rollback re-points traffic at the previous release, which is kept warm for one
hour after a deploy. After that hour it becomes an ordinary deploy of the older
build and takes just as long as one.

# Incident response

## Severity levels
Severity one is a full outage or a confirmed data exposure. Severity two is a
degraded service with a workaround. Severity three is a defect with no customer
impact and is handled in the ordinary queue.

## Paging on call
Severity one and severity two reach the on-call engineer immediately, at any hour
of the day or night. Severity three never does. Anyone may raise the severity of
an incident; only the incident commander may lower it.

## Status page updates
The status page is updated within fifteen minutes of a severity-one declaration
and every thirty minutes after that until it is resolved, even when there is
nothing new to say.

## Postmortems
Every severity-one incident gets a written postmortem within five working days. A
postmortem names causes and never names a person as one.

queries.query: how long does a refund take to come back
queries.note: Only the refunds section states the five-to-ten-day figure. One of the two queries where the arms disagree: measured at k=5 the vector arm puts it first, BM25 third, and fusion second.

queries.query: what happens when my card is declined
queries.note: The dunning section is the answer and shares not one content word with the query - it says 'When a charge fails'. Kept deliberately: measured at k=5, every lexical arm misses it, and a fixture with no misses in it would be measuring the labeller rather than the retriever.

queries.query: if I upgrade halfway through the month am I charged twice
queries.note: Proration is answered only under 'Changing your plan', which spells out 'never charged twice for the same days'.
A bare identifier: the case BM25 exists for. The rate-limit doc explains the same behaviour but the error reference is what the query asks for.

queries.query: my key is valid but the call is refused
queries.note: ERR_4033 is role-based refusal; ERR_4010 (invalid credential) is the distractor and shares most of its vocabulary.

queries.query: which failures are safe to retry
queries.note: The retry guidance section; every other section mentions retrying too.

queries.query: I lost my api key can I look it up again
queries.note: Answered by 'stores only a hash of it', with no shared wording.

queries.query: rotate an api key without downtime
queries.note: A measured miss for both arms, and an instructive one. The shared tokenizer stems 'rotating' (in the heading) to 'rotat' but leaves the query's 'rotate' alone, so the two never meet; 'downtime' is 'a gap in service' in the text. Both arms return the neighbouring 'API keys' section instead. The label stays where it is: the rotation section is the answer whether or not the retriever can find it.

queries.query: sign in from a machine with no browser
queries.note: The device flow, and the command that starts it. Both genuinely answer.

queries.query: how many requests per minute on the team plan
queries.note: The quota table section.

queries.query: does issuing more keys give us more capacity
queries.note: Same section, different question; the answer sentence is explicit.

queries.query: is a slow endpoint treated as a failure
queries.note: Stated directly in the registration section.

queries.query: how do I check a webhook really came from you
queries.note: The third measured miss, and the one that is about chunking rather than vocabulary: the signature-verification section never contains the word 'webhook' - that word is in the document title, which sectioning leaves out of the body. A chunk stripped of the context that named it is the classic retrieval failure, so it is in the fixture on purpose.

queries.query: stop someone replaying a captured delivery
queries.note: Replay protection via the timestamp.

queries.query: remove access when an employee leaves
queries.note: SCIM does deprovisioning; the just-in-time section says why it cannot.

queries.query: what stops us being locked out if the identity provider breaks
queries.note: Break-glass owners keep password login.

queries.query: how long is the export download link good for
queries.note: Seven days, in the retention section.

queries.query: can I undo deleting a workspace
queries.note: The thirty-day grace period.

queries.query: why is my export not a csv file
queries.note: The formats section explains the nested-record reason.

queries.query: roll back a bad release
queries.note: Both content terms are in the rollback section.

queries.query: when does an instance get taken out of rotation
queries.note: Three consecutive health check failures.

queries.query: target staging instead of production from the command line
queries.note: The --environment flag on deploy; the deployments doc talks about environments at length and is the distractor that every arm ranks first. The second query where the arms disagree below rank 1.

queries.query: does the tool need a language runtime installed
queries.note: 'no runtime dependencies ... without installing a language runtime'.

queries.query: who gets woken up in the middle of the night
queries.note: A near miss worth keeping: 'night' is the ONLY term the query and the answer share, and on that single term both arms rank the paging section third rather than first. Lexical retrieval scraping through on one word is not the same thing as lexical retrieval working.

queries.query: how often do we update the status page during an outage
queries.note: Fifteen minutes, then every thirty.
